title: A hot cup is part of the surroundings
stem: 50.0 cm³ of 1.20 mol dm⁻³ HCl and 50.0 cm³ of 0.800 mol dm⁻³ NaOH are mixed in an insulated cup. Both start at 22.0 °C and the corrected maximum is 28.0 °C. Take final solution mass as 100.0 g, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, and cup heat capacity as 45.0 J K⁻¹. The curve shows a constructed temperature trace. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the limiting reagent and calculate the reaction heat, including the cup.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the molar enthalpy change per mole of water formed. Explain its sign.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess a calculation that ignores both the cup and the limiting reagent, using all the HCl moles.

steps.text: n(H⁺) = 0.0600 mol and n(OH⁻) = 0.0400 mol; OH⁻ is limiting.
Heat gained by solution is 100.0×4.18×6.0 = 2508 J.
The cup gains 45.0×6.0 = 270 J; q(reaction) = −2778 J.
Water formed is 0.0400 mol, so divide reaction heat by this amount, not total acid.
The chemical system transfers energy to the solution/cup, so the reaction is exothermic.
Ignoring the cup misses heat absorbed by the surroundings.
Using excess-acid moles overstates the reacting amount; both errors make the magnitude too small.

title: Extrapolating a cooling line to the mixing instant
stem: A model experiment reacts 0.0250 mol of solid with excess solution at time t = 0. The solution/cup effective heat capacity is 334.4 J K⁻¹ and its initial temperature is 22.0 °C. Post-reaction readings at t = 2, 4, 6 minutes are 31.8, 31.6, 31.4 °C. Assume this cooling trend is linear and valid back to t = 0. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the corrected temperature rise and reaction enthalpy.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using 31.8 °C as the maximum gives a different result. Calculate that result and the percentage underestimate in magnitude.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one condition that would invalidate the straight-line correction, and explain its effect on confidence in the result.

steps.text: The post-reaction slope is −0.100 °C min⁻¹.
Extrapolating gives T(0) = 32.0 °C and ΔT = 10.0 K.
Compare heat magnitudes using (10.0−9.8)/10.0.
The magnitude is underestimated by 2.00%.
If reaction continues throughout the post-reaction measurements, they combine ongoing heat release with cooling.
The fitted line then does not represent cooling alone, so its intercept cannot be accepted as a corrected instantaneous maximum.

title: Separating dissolving from neutralising
stem: Two supplied processes have enthalpy changes: NaOH(s) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq), −44.0 kJ mol⁻¹; NaOH(s) + H⁺(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + H₂O(l), −102.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The same final ionic states and temperature apply in both processes. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the cycle to determine ΔH for H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the temperature rise when 0.0300 mol NaOH(s) reacts with excess acid and the effective heat capacity is 250 J K⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the cycle cannot be used without checking the states and concentrations of the final ions.

steps.text: Reverse dissolution: Na⁺ + OH⁻ → NaOH(s), + 44.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
Add it to the supplied solid–acid reaction, cancelling NaOH(s) and Na⁺.
Neutralisation ΔH = −102.0 + 44.0 = −58.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
The full solid-to-final reaction releases 0.0300×102.0 = 3.06 kJ.
Using only the neutralisation enthalpy would omit the energy released during dissolution.
Hess’s law compares identical initial and final thermodynamic states.
Different solution concentrations or physical states can include additional dilution/phase-change enthalpies.
An unaccounted state difference is an extra process, not a failure of energy conservation.

title: Which bonds actually change during hydrogenation?
stem: Consider C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g). Supplied average bond enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹ are C = C 614, C−C 348, H−H 436 and C−H 414. A measured gas-phase reaction enthalpy is −137 kJ mol⁻¹. The structural diagram distinguishes unchanged and changed bonding. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the reaction enthalpy using bond enthalpies, explicitly counting the changed bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student also counts all four original C−H bonds as broken. Explain how a complete correct bond inventory handles these bonds.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the estimate with the measured result and explain why the difference is plausible.

steps.text: Break one C = C and one H−H bond: 614 + 436 = 1050 kJ mol⁻¹.
Form one C−C and two additional C−H bonds: 348 + 2×414 = 1176 kJ mol⁻¹.
A full inventory may break all reactant bonds, but it must also form all six product C−H bonds.
Four C−H contributions then cancel between broken and formed bonds.
The net inventory remains one C = C plus one H−H broken, and one C−C plus two C−H formed.
The estimate is 11 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic.
Average bond enthalpies refer to gaseous bonds averaged across different chemical environments.
The particular C−H/C−C environments in these molecules need not have precisely those average values.

title: A reaction-coordinate drawing is not a cooling curve
stem: The supplied potential-energy profile represents A(g) → B(g). The reactant level is + 20 kJ mol⁻¹, the product level is −15 kJ mol⁻¹, and the peak is + 80 kJ mol⁻¹, all relative to the same reference. The vertical levels refer to one mole of reaction as written. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine ΔH for the forward and reverse reactions, then the heat for converting 2.00 mol A at constant pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain both the direction of energy transfer and the greater relative stability of one side.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A catalyst lowers the peak to + 50 kJ mol⁻¹. Assess claims that it changes the heat released or halves the reaction time.

steps.text: Forward ΔH = E(products)−E(reactants) = −15−20.
Forward ΔH = −35.0 and reverse ΔH = + 35.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
Converting 2.00 mol releases 70.0 kJ, so q(system) = −70.0 kJ.
Energy transfers from the chemical system to the surroundings in the forward direction.
The products have lower potential energy than the reactants.
Thus B is more stable in this enthalpic comparison; stability here does not mean the reverse reaction is impossible.
ΔH remains −35.0 kJ mol⁻¹ because both endpoint levels are unchanged.
A lower barrier can increase rate, but profile heights alone do not establish that time is exactly halved.
The horizontal axis is reaction coordinate, so its length cannot be read as reaction time.

title: The energy and oxygen cost of incomplete combustion
stem: One mole of CH₄ is burnt. Analysis shows 75.0% of its carbon becomes CO₂ and 25.0% becomes CO, with no soot and all hydrogen forming liquid water. Supplied heats released are 890 kJ per mole CH₄ for complete combustion and 607 kJ per mole CH₄ when CO is the carbon product. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the heat released and the percentage energy shortfall relative to complete combustion.

parts.label: c

steps.text: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O and CH₄ + 1.5 O₂ → CO + 2 H₂O.
Weight their oxygen requirements by carbon fractions 0.750 and 0.250.
Oxygen consumed = 0.750×2 + 0.250×1.5 = 1.875 mol.
Heat released = 819 kJ; the reaction heat is −819 kJ.
Some carbon leaves as toxic CO rather than harmlessly disappearing.
CO can subsequently oxidise to CO₂, releasing the remaining chemical energy elsewhere.
The useful energy per mole fuel is also reduced, potentially requiring more fuel for the same service.

title: Hydrogen utilisation in an acidic fuel cell
stem: An acidic hydrogen fuel cell receives 1.00 mol H₂. Only 80.0% reacts; the rest exits unreacted. For reacted hydrogen, 60.0% of the supplied 286 kJ mol⁻¹ reaction energy becomes useful electrical energy. The diagram shows the material streams, not membrane construction. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write balanced oxidation and reduction half-equations and the overall equation per mole H₂.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine water formed, oxygen consumed and useful electrical energy from the feed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish the quoted conversion efficiency from overall feed-to-electricity efficiency. Explain one condition needed before calling hydrogen a renewable fuel.

steps.text: Oxidation: H₂ → 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻.
Reduction: 0.5 O₂ + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → H₂O.
Overall: H₂ + 0.5 O₂ → H₂O.
Reacted H₂ = 0.800 mol; water formed = 0.800 mol and O₂ consumed = 0.400 mol.
Useful energy = 0.800×286×0.600.
Useful electrical energy = 137 kJ.
Overall feed-to-electricity efficiency = 0.800×0.600 = 48.0%.
The 60.0% applies to energy of reacted hydrogen, while unreacted feed carries chemical energy out.
Hydrogen must be produced using replenished low-carbon energy/resources; the fuel-cell exhaust alone does not establish its source is renewable.

title: A methanol fuel cell in an alkaline electrolyte
stem: An alkaline methanol fuel cell has oxidation half-equation CH₃OH + 6 OH⁻ → CO₂ + 5 H₂O + 6 e⁻. Methanol has molar mass 32.0 g mol⁻¹ and supplied reaction energy 726 kJ mol⁻¹. At 45.0% conversion to useful electricity, the device must deliver 500 kJ. Assume complete utilisation and treat the immediate carbon product as CO₂. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Balance the oxygen reduction half-equation and deduce the overall reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the required methanol mass and the amount of immediate CO₂ formed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the hydroxide ions cancel from the overall equation but are still needed in the half-equations.

steps.text: Use O₂, H₂O and e⁻ on the left and OH⁻ on the right.
Reduction: 1.5 O₂ + 3 H₂O + 6 e⁻ → 6 OH⁻.
Adding gives CH₃OH + 1.5 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O.
Required reacted methanol = 500/(0.450×726).
n(CH₃OH) = 1.53046 mol and mass = 49.0 g.
CO₂ formed = 1.53 mol, since the overall reaction has a 1:1 carbon ratio.
They carry/participate in charge-balanced electrode reactions in the specified alkaline medium.
Equal amounts are consumed and produced in the two half-equations, so their net amount is unchanged.
Cancelling them from the sum does not justify writing unbalanced individual electron-transfer steps.

title: A magnesium oxide cycle with a hidden direction
stem: The supplied reaction enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹ are: Mg(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g), −467; MgO(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l), −146; H₂(g) + 0.5 O₂(g) → H₂O(l), −286. All matched aqueous states are identical. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Combine the equations to obtain Mg(s) + 0.5 O₂(g) → MgO(s), showing the necessary reversal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the heat released when 0.480 g pure Mg is converted completely; use M(Mg) = 24.0 g mol⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why leaving the −146 value unchanged when reversing that equation violates energy conservation.

steps.text: Add the magnesium–acid and hydrogen–oxygen reactions.
Reverse the MgO–acid equation, changing its enthalpy to + 146.
HCl, MgCl₂, H₂ and H₂O cancel to give the stated target.
Heat released = 0.0200×607 = 12.1 kJ; reaction heat = −12.1 kJ.
A process followed by its exact reverse must have zero net enthalpy change.
Keeping the same sign would assign a nonzero enthalpy to a cycle returning to its starting state.
The direction of energy transfer reverses when the process is reversed.

title: Calibrating the apparatus before measuring a reaction
stem: An electrical heater supplies 12.0 J s⁻¹ for 240 s to the same filled calorimeter used later. Temperature rises from 20.0 to 28.0 °C. Assume all electrical energy is absorbed, with negligible heat loss. A subsequent reaction of 0.0200 mol has corrected temperature rise 5.50 K. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the effective heat capacity of the filled calorimeter and the reaction enthalpy.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A calculation using only solution mass 100 g and c 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ gives a different capacity. Explain why these data cannot all describe the stated loss-free calibration.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why repeating the calibration with a different solution mass would be necessary.

steps.text: Calibration energy = 12.0×240 = 2880 J.
Effective heat capacity = 2880/8.0 = 360 J K⁻¹.
Reaction heat = −360×5.50 = −1980 J.
Molar enthalpy = −1.980/0.0200 = −99.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
The solution alone would have heat capacity 418 J K⁻¹, already exceeding 360 J K⁻¹.
Adding a physical cup can only increase the total positive heat capacity.
At least one mass/property/energy/temperature assumption or measurement must therefore be wrong.
The solution contribution to heat capacity is proportional to mass.
The effective constant belongs to the full cup-plus-contents setup, not only to the empty container.

stem: Estimate C₂H₅OH(g) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(g) using average bond enthalpies(kJ mol⁻¹): C−H414, C−C348, C−O358, O−H463, O = O498, C = O in CO₂804. An additional supplied process is H₂O(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −44.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the supplied phase change to estimate the reaction enthalpy when the three moles of water are liquid, with ethanol still gaseous.

parts.label: c

Total broken energy = 4733 kJ mol⁻¹.

A supplied ethanol vaporisation/condensation enthalpy is required before the state-function comparison is valid.

title: Formation data and the chosen water state
stem: Supplied standard formation enthalpies(kJ mol⁻¹) are ethanol(l)−278, CO₂(g)−394, H₂O(l)−286 and H₂O(g)−242. Oxygen is in its standard elemental state. Consider complete combustion of one mole ethanol. Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the combustion equation producing liquid water and calculate its standard enthalpy change.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recalculate for gaseous water and interpret the difference.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why assigning zero formation enthalpy to ethanol because it is in its standard state is incorrect.

steps.text: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 3 H₂O(l).
Use sum of product formation enthalpies minus sum of reactant formation enthalpies, including coefficients.
Unrounded ΔH° = 2(−394) + 3(−286)−(−278) = −1368 kJ mol⁻¹; reported result≈−1.37×10³ kJ mol⁻¹.
Replace only the water formation value by−242.
Unrounded ΔH° = −1236 kJ mol⁻¹; reported result≈−1.24×10³ kJ mol⁻¹.
Gaseous water retains 132 kJ mol⁻¹ more enthalpy per mole ethanol; condensation of three moles water releases that difference.
Zero standard formation enthalpy is assigned to an element in its reference standard state.
Ethanol is a compound; being a pure liquid standard state does not make its formation enthalpy zero.
Its formation equation is 2 C(graphite) + 3 H₂(g) + 0.5 O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l).

title: A divalent cation in a supplied Born–Haber cycle
stem: For MgCl₂(s), ΔHf° = −642 kJ mol⁻¹. Supplied cycle steps(kJ mol⁻¹ formula units) are Mg(s) → Mg(g):148; Mg ionisation energies 738 and 1451; Cl₂(g) → 2 Cl(g):244; Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g):−349 per mole chlorine atoms. parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine lattice formation and lattice dissociation enthalpies.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the two distinct errors in using only 738 and one−349 term.

steps.text: Include 148 + 738 + 1451 for magnesium and 244 for two chlorine atoms.
Two chloride ions require 2(−349).
Total = 1883 kJ mol⁻¹.
Cycle relation:−642 = 1883 + ΔHlatt, formation.
Lattice formation enthalpy = −2525 kJ mol⁻¹.
Lattice dissociation enthalpy = + 2525 kJ mol⁻¹.
Mg²⁺ formation requires removing a second electron, so the 1451 term is essential.
Ea ch MgCl₂ formula unit contains two chloride ions, so two electron-affinity processes are required.
Ignoring these terms changes the thermochemical path and cannot preserve the formation enthalpy sum.

title: The second electron affinity has the opposite sign
stem: For Na₂O(s), ΔHf° = −414 kJ mol⁻¹. Supplied steps(kJ mol⁻¹) are Na atomisation 108, first Na ionisation 496, O₂ bond dissociation 498, first oxygen electron affinity−141 and second oxygen electron affinity + 744. The supplied cycle starts with 2 Na(s) + 0.5 O₂(g). Give calculated answers to three significant figures unless a different precision is requested.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the enthalpy needed to reach 2 Na⁺(g) + O²⁻(g).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate lattice formation enthalpy and explain how a positive second affinity can coexist with stable solid formation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate replacing the two affinity values by twice−141.

steps.text: Sodium contribution = 2(108 + 496) = 1208 kJ mol⁻¹.
Oxygen contribution = 0.5(498)−141 + 744 = 852 kJ mol⁻¹.
Total = 2060 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔHlatt, formation = −414−2060 = −2474 kJ mol⁻¹.
Adding an electron to a negative gaseous ion is opposed by electrostatic repulsion, so that isolated step is endothermic.
Strong energy release when the ionic lattice forms more than compensates for the energy-demanding steps.
The replacement gives−282 instead of + 603, an error of 885 kJ mol⁻¹.

Successive affinities describe different initial species and cannot be assumed equal.
